measure.title: PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

terms.plain: These include retirement savings, investments, business interests, belongings, and other property besides real estate.
These are rules in California’s Constitution.

summary.text: Bans new taxes on owning personal assets and taxes based on past activities or status.
summary.more: Applies to state laws and constitutional provisions enacted from January 1, 2026; leaves existing taxes and real estate taxation unchanged. Emergency taxes may reach back 365 days, with revenue going to the declared emergency response.

quotes.text: No state law and no provision of this Constitution … enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly. … Nothing in this section shall alter or limit the imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025. … Nothing in this section shall alter or affect the … taxation of real property as provided in other provisions … of this Constitution.

No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date of the state law or constitutional provision. … Nothing in subdivision (a) shall alter or limit the imposition or collection of any tax that was in effect, imposed, and first collected on or before December 31, 2025.

Subdivision (a) shall not apply to a tax imposed by a … statute passed by the Legislature on or after January 1, … 2026, where both of the following apply: … The tax does not apply retroactively for more than … 365 days prior to the date the statute takes effect. … At least one of the following conditions exists: … The Governor declares an emergency as a result of … a fire, flood, storm, civil disorder, earthquake, volcanic … eruption, or actual or imminent attack by a foreign … enemy, and the use of the revenues from the tax are … expressly limited by the statute to responding to the … emergency. … The Governor declares a fiscal emergency pursuant … to subdivision (f) of Section 10 of Article IV and the use … of the revenues from the tax are expressly limited by the … statute to responding to the fiscal emergency.

“Retirement holdings, individually owned assets, … and other forms of personal savings” means pensions; … retirement accounts including, but not limited to, … 401(k) accounts, 403(b) accounts, and all other … individual retirement accounts; mutual funds; and all … personal property, whether tangible or intangible, … including, but not limited to, financial assets, … investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, … intellectual property, personal belongings, and other … assets used to produce or collect income or savings for … retirement or financial planning.

edges.why: There is no current ownership tax on financial assets, but the question concerns future protection.
This claim places funding healthcare above protecting extreme wealth from an ownership tax.
Existing ownership taxes provide context without resolving whether the tax principle is fair.
The text preserves limited retroactivity for emergency response.
Restricting revenue options could constrain future funding, though the scale is unclear.
Protecting savers is the claimed benefit of giving up these revenue options.
The Analyst identifies Prop 40 as a potential application of this conflict rule.
This claim concerns the healthcare consequences of blocking the billionaire tax.
The finding describes the kind of risk the campaign claims proposals create, without verifying those proposals.
The claimed double taxation is a future possibility, not a current tax on financial ownership.
The analysis identifies possible lower revenue but does not estimate healthcare losses.
Blocking Prop 40 is a conditional legal possibility, not an assured outcome.
